statement: University education should be free for every student, with the full cost paid by the government.
question: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
model:
Whether higher education should be funded entirely from taxation is one of the more divisive questions in public policy. While I accept that removing tuition fees altogether would place a heavy burden on the state, I largely agree that university should be free at the point of use, because the benefits extend well beyond the individual graduate.

The strongest argument for free tuition is that talent is distributed evenly across society, whereas wealth is not. When students must borrow tens of thousands of pounds, those from low-income families are understandably more reluctant to take the risk, and a gifted teenager may settle for an unskilled job simply to avoid debt. Countries such as Germany and Finland, which charge little or nothing, have shown that open access need not lower standards; if anything, it widens the pool from which future doctors, engineers and teachers are drawn.

Furthermore, a highly educated workforce is a public good rather than a private luxury. Graduates tend to earn more and therefore pay more tax over their lifetimes, so the state recovers a considerable part of its investment indirectly. They are also more likely to vote, to volunteer and to raise children who value learning, effects that are difficult to price but undeniably valuable.

That said, unlimited free provision carries real dangers. If every course is funded regardless of its quality or relevance, universities may expand programmes that attract applicants but lead to few employment opportunities. A sensible compromise would be to fund tuition fully while linking the number of places in each subject to national needs and to graduates' outcomes.

In conclusion, although the expense cannot be ignored, I believe that governments should cover the cost of university education, provided that the money is spent with discipline. Treating degrees as a shared investment, rather than a personal purchase, is ultimately fairer and more productive for society as a whole.
